MANAGEMENT BOARD DECISION 6/2025 of 26 March 2025 adopting the profiles to be made available to the European Border and Coast Guard standing corps for 2026
Having regard to the European Border and Coast Guard Regulation1 (hereinafter ‘the Regulation’), in particular Article 100(2)(i) thereof, Whereas:

(1) In accordance with Article 54(4) of the Regulation, the Management Board, on the basis of a proposal by the Executive Director taking into account the Agency’s risk analysis, the results of the vulnerability assessment and the multiannual strategic policy for European integrated border management, and building on the numbers and profiles of staff available to the Agency through its statutory staff and ongoing secondments, by 31 March of each year, should adopt a decision, inter alia, defining the profiles of, and setting the requirements for, operational staff.

(2) The profiles of operational staff represent the competences required from staff of the European Border and Coast Guard standing corps deployed as members of the teams (hereinafter ‘standing corps’) to carry out border control and return tasks, including those requiring executive powers, and constitute a principal basis of the Agency’s capability planning and the establishment of pools for operational activities.

(3) All members of the standing corps may, additionally to their profile, be assigned to perform operational horizontal functions within the standing corps as defined in Management Board Decision 18/20242. The roles and responsibilities related to operational horizontal functions concern the management of operational staff deployed as members of the teams and shall therefore not be covered in this Decision.

(4) Pursuant to the second subparagraph of Article 82(6) of the Regulation, by way of derogation from the first subparagraph of Article 82(6), the decision of the Management Board referred to in point (a) of Article 54(4) of the Regulation shall indicate the profiles to which the obligation to wear a uniform does not apply due to the specific nature of the operational activity.
(5) Provisions set out in points (b), (c) and (e) of Article 54(4) of the Regulation shall be addressed with a separate Management Board Decision to be adopted no later than 31 March 2025.

1 Regulation (EU) 2019/1896 of 13 November 2019 on the European Border and Coast Guard (OJ L 295, 14.11.2019, p.1). 2 Management Board Decision 18/2024 of 27 March 2024 on operational horizontal functions within the European Border and Coast Guard standing corps.
Article 1 – Profiles and derogations from the obligation to wear uniform

The profiles of, and the requirements for, operational staff within the European Border and Coast Guard standing corps, as well as the derogation from the obligation to wear uniform, as set out in the Annex to this Decision, are hereby adopted.
This decision enters into force on the day following its adoption.
Annex: Profiles to be made available to the European Border and Coast Guard standing corps in 2026 and derogations from the obligation to wear uniform

A Border and Coast Guard Officer is an official of a competent national authority of a MS or a member of the Agency’s statutory staff who carries out border control tasks within the meaning of the Schengen Borders Code4 or who supports tasks related to European coast guard functions, especially maritime border control and search and rescue, and therefore performs at least one of the core tasks of the profile. A Border and Coast Guard Officer may also be able to perform one or more of the profile’s auxiliary tasks.
2.2.1. Border checks (First line, gate and second line checks)
a) To check at the external borders of a MS if a person is authorised to enter or leave the territory of the country, as stipulated by the Schengen Borders Code and the operational plan.
b) To refer cases to the second line of expertise, when deemed necessary. 2.2.1.2. Border checks (Second line)

a) To perform thorough checks and additional verifications by using technical devices and by further consulting the relevant databases, as well as including on the supporting of the recognition of motor vehicle crimes and related documents and referring them to the national authorities, when applicable.
b) To assess the authenticity of documents and if they are presented by the rightful holder.

c) To contribute to verifying the traveller’s declarations with the aim to assess the purpose and conditions of the intended stay, including checking supporting documents (accommodation, guarantee of return…) and means of subsistence.
d) To support, if required, the production of alerts aiming at the dissemination of the findings, trends and routes.
e) To support first line border checks. 2.2.2. Border surveillance
a) To carry out border surveillance in a designated area at the external borders of the MS and in third countries.
b) To operate relevant technical equipment (terrestrial assets, portable equipment, etc.).
c) To detect and apprehend persons having crossed or having attempted to cross the border irregularly.
d) To document all relevant actions by using methods and technology (reports, videos, photos, etc.).
e) To support the prevention and detection of cross-border crime.

4 Article 2(10), (11) and (12) of Regulation (EU) 2016/399 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 9 March 2016 on a Union Code on the rules governing the movement of persons across borders (Schengen Borders Code) (OJ L 77, 23.3.2016, p. 1).

a) To participate in the Agency’s maritime operational activities (i.e. joint operations, multipurpose maritime operations and other related activities) in order to assist and support the activities related to European coast guard functions.

b) To facilitate cooperation, information exchange and sharing of best practices between Frontex, EMSA and EFCA and competent national authorities responsible for coast guard functions in the context of Frontex-coordinated operational activities.
c) To support the host country’s maritime surveillance activities by operating dedicated technical equipment, information platforms and services provided by the Agency.
d) To support border control authorities in detection of maritime cross-border crimes related to other coast guard authorities’ responsibilities.

e) To support all relevant staff deployed in the Agency’s maritime operational activities in the preparation and delivery of reports related to coast guard functions, such as the sighting forms on fisheries and potential marine pollution. f)

To support the practical implementation of activities under the European Multidisciplinary Platform Against Criminal Threats (‘EMPACT’) linked with coast guard functions in which the Agency is involved.

a) To carry out interviews by applying appropriate interview techniques, and in compliance with fundamental rights, in order to establish the assumed nationality of a person without valid identification document having crossed, or having attempted to cross, the external border of a MS.
b) To carry out screening interviews by applying the appropriate interview techniques. 2.3.2. Registration and fingerprinting
a) To operate fingerprinting technology and equipment.

b) To take and record legible fingerprints of persons who have irregularly crossed the external border of the MS or applied for international protection and perform the related tasks in the relevant databases.
c) To support the host MS in issuing documents for registered persons.
To perform return-related tasks as a member of a team in non-complex, routine situations, such as:
a) To provide support to Frontex Return Escort and Support Officers in the implementation of returns, including returns by air, sea and land.
b) To provide support to Return Specialists in organising and implementing return-related tasks under their competences.
c) To provide administrative and operational assistance during the organisation or implementation of other return-related activities.
A Border and Coast Guard Officer in the standing corps should: •
• Have adequate knowledge of the English language (equivalent to Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (‘CEFR’) level B1 for 2.2.1. and 2.2.2, or CEFR level B2 for 2.2.3.).
Have proven professional experience related to coast guard functions activities and multipurpose maritime operations.

• Have experience in the implementation of common cross-sectoral (interagency cooperation) and cross-border (international or EU cooperation) mechanism for combatting risks and threats in the maritime domain.

• Proven professional experience working at air, land or sea border crossing points, performing external border or inland surveillance within the territory of a MS, or providing ground support to return operations.
• Ability to communicate effectively in languages spoken in third countries.
• Ability to perform the activities listed under auxiliary tasks (2.3.).
• Experience with de-escalation or mediation techniques and methodologies.
• Experience in working with information platforms and services of EFCA or EMSA.

An Information Officer is an official of a competent national authority of a MS or a member of the Agency’s statutory staff who supports information and data management processes (collection, assessment, analysis and distribution) between the Agency and national authorities (including third countries). An Information Officer carries out at least one of the following tasks:
3.2.1. Collection of information for situation monitoring
a) To monitor, collect and validate real-time operational information using a variety of sources, including aerial and maritime surveillance, satellite imagery and open sources.
b) To process and validate incidents in the Joint Operations Reporting Application (‘JORA’), crossreferencing with EUROSUR data, Frontex operational reports and other reliable sources.
c) To generate and distribute real-time operational and situational reports, alerts, and other relevant products to key stakeholders, while ensuring integration with the Agency’s reporting systems.
To support the execution of EUROSUR Fusion Services5, such as multipurpose aerial surveillance, vessel tracking, media monitoring and open-source intelligence, by:

a) Selective monitoring of designated third-country ports, coasts and areas in the maritime domain in order to detect, identify and track vessels and other craft being used for, or suspected of being used for, irregular migration or cross-border crime, including in the case of persons in distress at sea.

b) Monitoring of designated areas of air borders in order to detect, identify and track aircraft and other forms of equipment being used for, or suspected of being used for, irregular migration or cross-border crime.

c) Tracking of vessels or other craft over high seas and the tracking of aircraft, where those vessels, other craft or aircraft are suspected of, or have been identified as, being used for irregular migration or cross-border crime, including in the case of persons in distress at sea.

d) Selective monitoring of designated pre-frontier areas at the external borders which have been identified through risk analysis and information as being potential departure or transit areas for irregular migration or cross-border crime.
3.2.3. Operation and management of the Agency’s 24/7 Operations Centre

To support the provision of centralised coordination and management capability, including infrastructure and manpower with access to various EUROSUR Fusion Services (e.g. Multipurpose Aerial Surveillance), other integrated and tailor-made information products and sources of data and information (i.e. National Coordination Centres (‘NCC’), national authorities, Frontex Liaison Officers) as well as services executed in near real time or in real time on a tactical, operational and strategic level.
An Information Officer in the standing corps should: •
5 Applicable in instances in which EUROSUR Fusion Services are provided in the framework of an operational activity under an operational plan.
• Have an adequate knowledge of the English language (equivalent to CEFR level B2).
• Have an advanced level of knowledge of using common ICT software applications or Frontex Information Management Systems (e.g. EUROSUR Fusion Services, JORA, etc.).
• Experience in working in border management or law enforcement (i.e. cross-border crime etc.), a coast guard, air force, air traffic control or naval authority.
• Experience in working in a National Situation Centre, NCC, Rescue Coordination Centre, International Coordination Centre or other command and control centre.
• Ability to speak the language of the host country or the languages of certain third countries (such as Middle Eastern and North African countries), or knowledge of additional EU languages.

A Debriefing Officer is an official of a competent national authority of a MS or a member of the Agency’s statutory staff who performs either debriefing or screening interviews, or cultural mediation, by carrying out at least one of the following tasks:

a) To carry out voluntary, formal, anonymous and confidential debriefing interviews by applying adequate interviewing techniques to collect detailed information 6, including personal data related to persons who cross unauthorised the external borders in accordance with Article 88 of the Regulation, operational personal data related to suspects, victims, and witnesses of crossborder crime in accordance with Article 90 of the Regulation, and information on fundamental rights issues experienced during the journey or as push and pull factors.

b) To prepare reports of debriefing interviews to be sent to the host Member State and to the Agency via secured official communication channels agreed in the respective operational plan with the host country.

c) To use open sources to verify the information collected via debriefing interviews or to collect depersonalised additional data, that could supplement the information that has been collected via debriefing interviews.
d) To support the profiling of migrants and identify new modi operandi and migration trends used by irregular migrants and facilitators or criminal networks.
e) To obtain information regarding possible suspects involved in people smuggling or other crossborder crime, and to refer them to the second line or to specialised police. f)
To produce monthly and ad hoc reports based on the requirements of the Agency’s risk analysis entities and submit them according to the reporting flow established in each joint operation.

g) To support the proper sharing and dissemination of information provided by debriefing teams in the field, and to support the quality of debriefing and screening tasks by identifying and sharing best practices with debriefing teams.

h) To support training sessions, workshops and briefings or any other activities in which the Agency’s risk analysis entities7 participate in relation to the standing corps and debriefing activities. Screening i)

To carry out mandatory8 and formal screening interviews in compliance with fundamental rights by applying appropriate interview techniques in order to identify migration patterns used by irregular migrants.
To establish the assumed nationality of an interviewed person.
k) To collect information related to migrant profiles with a view of supporting the development of threat profiles.

6 The data listed in this paragraph shall not include the personal data of the interviewee. 7 As foreseen in Management Board Decision 45/2023 of 22 November 2023 on the new organisational structure of the Agency. 8 Subject to the national law of the host country.
To collect information at land, sea or air border crossing points as related to irregular migration and cross-border crime.
m) To produce monthly and ad hoc reports based on the requirements of the Agency’s risk analysis entities and submit them according to the reporting procedure established in each joint operation.

n) To support training sessions, workshops and briefings or any other activities in which the Agency’s risk analysis entities participate in relation to the standing corps and interviewing or screening activities. 4.2.2. Cultural mediation

a) To provide general support relating to cultural mediation, interpretation and or translation to the Agency’s debriefing and screening teams, and on request of their team leaders, to the national authorities in areas receiving irregular migrants who have crossed or are attempting to cross the external border.
b) To facilitate the communication between migrants and the members of the teams by using their expertise on culture and language.
c) To prepare relevant information to support the members of the teams in their activities (specific questions, background knowledge, or any important matter to consider during the interview).
d) To translate accurately and comprehensively from the English language into different migrants’ native languages and vice versa.

e) To monitor media and open sources in relation to migratory flows from countries of departure and transit identified by the Agency’s risk analysis entities and transmit the relevant information for risk analysis. f)
To produce monthly and ad hoc reports based on the requirements of the Agency’s risk analysis entities and submit them according to the reporting flow established in each joint operation.

g) To support training sessions, workshops and briefings or any other activities in which the Agency’s risk analysis entities participate in relation to the standing corps and interviewing or screening activities.
h) To support the creation of knowledge products by the Agency’s risk analysis entities and the update of debriefing manuals. i)
To participate in the Agency’s fact-finding missions in Member States and third countries, if needed.
A Debriefing Officer in the standing corps should: •
• Have adequate knowledge of the English language (equivalent to CEFR level B2).
• Have proven professional experience in preparing and leading interviews of third-country nationals.
• Demonstrate advanced knowledge of the latest migration trends.
• Have good observation and communication skills.
• Demonstrate knowledge of the geopolitical situation of countries of origin or transit.
Demonstrate advanced knowledge of modi operandi for organised crime.
• Demonstrate advanced cultural awareness of the countries of origin and transit.
• Demonstrate awareness and knowledge of travel patterns and modi operandi.
• Have the capability to withstand stress and strong emotional events.
In addition, the following would be of advantage for all Debriefing Officers: •
Ability to speak a language spoken in a third country or the country of foreseen deployment.
• Successful previous completion of the relevant profile training courses organised by the Agency for: o
Debriefing experts (the debriefing officer will undergo targeted training).
• Participation in workshops and awareness sessions relevant to the tasks described above.
• Previous deployment experience in Frontex-coordinated joint operations performing debriefing or interviewing and advanced level screening tasks.

An Advanced Level Document Officer is an official of a competent national authority of a MS or a member of the Agency’s statutory staff who carries out thorough examinations of a broad range of travel-related documents.
a) To assess the authenticity of documents through detailed examination and if they are presented by the rightful holder.
b) To operate specialised equipment for document examinations.
c) To report on the findings of document examinations.
d) To produce, if required, “alerts” aiming at the dissemination of the findings, trends and routes.
e) To perform training for first line officers and other relevant staff. f)
To refer documents to the third line of expertise.

g) When deployed to airports, to carry out gate checks, conduct a pre-boarding examination of the passenger list, briefly interview target passengers, and quickly verify their travel documents including flight tickets and other supporting documents, under the supervision of local border guards.
An Advanced Level Document Officer in the standing corps should: •
Have proven professional experience of at least three years as a document examination officer.
• Have adequate knowledge of the English language (equivalent to CEFR level B2).
• Have knowledge of databases related to the examination of travel-related documents.
• Have participated in a training on advanced skills for the detection of falsified documents.
• Professional experience of working at air, land or sea border crossing points.
• Ability to communicate effectively in languages spoken in third countries.
• Experience in using databases and information management systems.

A Cross-Border Crime Detection Officer is an official of a competent national authority of a MS or a member of the Agency’s statutory staff who supports the national authorities of the host MS in the prevention, detection and combatting of serious crime with a cross-border dimension including terrorism or who carries out thorough verifications of vehicles and their documents in order to establish possible vehicle theft and trafficking. A Cross-Border Crime Detection Officer performs at least one of the following tasks:

a) To reinforce the tactical and operational border control measures in the prevention and detection of cross-border crime, in particular migrant smuggling, trafficking in human beings, and motor vehicle crime.

b) To support and advise officers working in the first line of information on the collection of evidence and other immediate measures of incidents related to cross-border crime to safeguard any investigative measures by the competent national authorities.
c) To become familiar with cross-border crime indicators and modi operandi and support the collection of relevant information for risk analysis.

d) To contribute to and encourage cooperation between competent authorities, and to facilitate the exchange of expertise and experience in the prevention, detection and combatting of crossborder crime.
e) To support first and second line border checks with the objective of preventing and detecting cross-border crime and identifying potential suspects and victims as well as witnesses. f)
To support border control by means of operating dedicated technical solutions and tools of the Agency.
g) To support the practical implementation of EMPACT activities in which the Agency is involved. 6.2.2. Motor vehicle crime detection
a) To recognise motor vehicle crimes and related documents and refer them to the national authorities.
b) To effectively use relevant Union, national and international databases.
c) To use technical equipment supporting the detection of motor vehicle crime.
d) To recognise emerging patterns of motor vehicle theft and report on them accordingly.
A Cross-Border Crime Detection Officer in the standing corps should: •

Have proven professional experience in the prevention, detection or combatting of cross-border crime, or the identification of suspected individuals involved in migrant smuggling, trafficking in human beings or other types of cross-border crime.
• Have adequate knowledge of the English language (CEFR level B2).
Specific to motor vehicle crime detection (6.2.2.): •
Have proven professional experience in dealing with the detection of motor vehicle crimes.
• Have adequate knowledge of the English language (CEFR level B1).
• At least two years of experience in the identification of suspected individuals involved in migrant smuggling, trafficking in human beings, or other types of cross-border crime.
• At least two years of experience in the prevention, detection and combatting of crime, especially serious crime with a cross-border dimension.
• Knowledge on the detection of motor vehicle crimes and forgery of travel documents as well as modus operandi applied for smuggling of illicit goods.
• At least three years of working experience in dealing with the detection of motor vehicle crimes or stolen boats.

A Dog Handler is an official of a competent national authority of a MS or a member of the Agency’s statutory staff who carries out border control at the external borders of the MS with the support of a service dog, performing at least one of the following tasks:
a) To perform border control tasks.
b) To search for and passively and proactively identify source(s) of human scent and use force in accordance with applicable legislation (the use of force not being mandatory).
c) To search for and indicate sources of product scent (e.g. explosives, narcotics).
d) To search for and indicate sources of bio-scent (e.g. blood, cadavers).
A Dog Handler in the standing corps should:
a) Have proven operational experience as a dog handler in competent national authority.
b) Have adequate knowledge of the English language (CEFR level B1).
c) Possess specific knowledge, skills, and competence as relevant to the respective tasks described in the Common Core Curriculum. In addition, the following would be an advantage:
a) At least two years of operational experience as a dog handler in a competent national authority.
b) Previous national assessment by a Frontex-certified national instructor based on the Agency’s standards.
c) Previous attendance of a centralised Frontex EBCGT training and evaluation session, and successful certification.
8. Logistics and Occupational Safety and Health Support Officer

A Logistics and Occupational Safety and Health Support Officer is an official of a competent national authority of a MS or a member of the Agency’s statutory staff who supports the Agency in the implementation of operational activities by providing logistical and organisational support to the Agency’s operational assets, or coordinating the implementation of the Agency’s occupational safety and health policies, by performing at least one of the following tasks:
a) To provide logistical and practical support in the deployment of human resources and technical equipment and supply and service delivery.
b) To liaise with internal and external stakeholders, including the organisation of logistics meetings, updates, and briefings.

c) To provide infrastructure management for permanent (buildings) and temporary (mobile office containers) facilities, including renting, installation, reinstallation, maintenance, equipment, provisions, monitoring, recording and accurately reporting on related information projects, tasks, and activities.

d) To provide inventory management of Frontex-owned, co-owned or leased technical equipment including deployment, redeployment, warehousing, asset and material management, maintenance management, status reporting, storage, and distribution.

e) To provide material management, storage, supply, resupply, replenishment and distribution of material, non-asset items, consumable items, personal protective equipment, Tactical Emergency Casualty Care (TECC) and other supplies and items. f)
To organise, coordinate, and monitor the provision of services.

g) To perform the weapons and ammunition inventory management, including weapons and ammunition assignment, withdrawal, recovery, storage, maintenance inspection, storage conditions, storage security assessments, as well as distribution and provision of weapons and ammunition supporting equipment.

h) To provide transportation and mobility assets management (vehicles, patrol cars, air and sea transportation means) including distribution, allocation, deployment, maintenance, resupply of related equipment and supplies (fuel, accessories, etc.), and services (insurance, etc.), ensure vehicle roadworthiness and the safe use of other transportation means. i)
To provide recommendations on supply chain management plans (demand, supply, replenishment, and safety stock), budgets and schedules.
a) To cooperate, to coordinate and to exchange information on occupational safety and health where the Agency shares a workplace.9
b) To implement the Agency’s prevention policy.10
c) To investigate workplace accidents and incidents, organise workplace visits, promote preventive measures and contribute to risk assessment.

9 Council Directive 89/391/EEC of 12 June 1989 on the introduction of measures to encourage improvements in the safety and health of workers at work, Official Journal of the European Communities, (OJ L 183 29.6.1989, p. 1). 10 Decision of the Executive Director R-ED-2022-145 of 22 August 2022 on operational Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) for the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (‘OSH Policy 2.0’).
d) To report to, and act as a point of contact for, the Agency’s central occupational safety and health entity.11
e) To monitor and analyse the application of relevant host country’s occupational safety and health legislation. f)
To monitor occupational safety and health on a local level.
g) To facilitate training, coaching, briefings, and information sessions to staff in occupational safety and health-related matters.
h) To manage personal protective equipment on a local level in cooperation with the Agency’s central logistics entity.12
A Frontex Logistics and Occupational Safety and Health Support Officer in the standing corps should: •
• Have adequate knowledge of English language (equivalent to CEFR level B2).
Specific to occupational safety and health support (9.2.3.): •
Have at least three years full-time proven experience in occupational safety and health.
11 As foreseen in Management Board Decision 45/2023. 12 As above.
9. Frontex Return Escort and Support Officer

A Frontex Return Escort and Support Officer is an official of a competent national authority of a MS or a member of the Agency’s statutory staff who provides support in the implementation of return operations and voluntary returns.
a) To support, by inter alia escorting or providing ground support, the implementation of all phases, including transits, of return operations and voluntary returns.
b) To provide ground support in the return of third-country nationals subject to a refusal of entry.13
c) To coordinate and facilitate the implementation of return operations.
d) To undertake administrative, operational and logistical tasks related to the implementation of return operations and voluntary returns.
e) To act as a member of a team supporting other officers when he or she has not been assigned to a particular third-country national to be returned. f)
To perform coordinating functions and provide operational and logistical support within the return team.
g) To act as a representative of Frontex on board of a return operation and voluntary return supported by Frontex.
h) To monitor, report on, and coordinate the implementation of return operations and voluntary returns. i)
To carry out return-related activities in the Agency’s central coordination hub for operational activities.14
A Frontex Return Escort and Support Officer in the standing corps should: •
Have adequate knowledge of the English language (equivalent to CEFR level B1).
Experience with de-escalation or mediation techniques and methodologies.
• Specific expertise in the protection of children and other persons in a vulnerable situation.
• Previous work experience in escorting or providing ground support.
13 Either as support in the return of third-country nationals who have been refused entry in accordance with Article 14 of the Regulation 2016/399

(Schengen Borders Code) who are subject to a return decision issued by the MS in accordance with the national law transposing Directive 2008/115/EC (Return Directive), or as support to national authorities responsible for the implementation of the Schengen Borders Code in this regard. 14 As foreseen in Management Board Decision 45/2023.

A Return Specialist is an official of a competent national authority of a MS or a member of the Agency’s statutory staff who carries out tasks connected to the return of third-country nationals illegally staying on the territory of a host MS. Return Specialists support the national authorities of MS or third countries (if applicable) responsible for return and reintegration in the following tasks:
a) To support in the identification and acquisition of travel documents from third-country authorities for the purpose of return and readmission.
b) To support in consular engagement for the purpose of identification and documentation of thirdcountry nationals under return process and of other return-related aspects.
c) To identify, collate and share best practices related to different aspects of third country cooperation in return.
d) To advise, support and inform on return capacity building in third countries.
e) To assist with case management in the relevant readmission case management systems (‘RCMS’). f)
To provide advisory support to the beneficiary in establishing an integrated and sustainable return management system. 10.2.2.
a) To provide return counselling to third-country nationals in both voluntary returns and (forced) return procedures.
b) To assess the needs during return counselling interviews and referring potential returnees to competent (national) authorities or potential reintegration partners.
c) To provide administrative and operational support to MS to facilitate the reintegration process, including assisting MS with the Frontex Reintegration Programme.
d) To provide assistance with the Reintegration Assistance Tool (‘RIAT’) for digital case management.
e) To identify, collect and share best practices related to return counselling and reintegration. f)
To advise, support and inform on reintegration capacity building projects in third countries of return. 10.2.3.
a) To process bookings in the Integrated Return Management Application (‘IRMA’) and the Frontex Application for Return (‘FAR’).
b) To assist with case management in RIAT.
c) To assist with case management in RCMS.
d) To provide support to return case management systems (RECAMAS), including alignment with the Frontex reference model and supporting the creation of synergies with IRMA.
e) To contribute to Frontex Return Data Collection in IRMA.
A Return Specialist in the standing corps should: •
Have an adequate knowledge of the English language (equivalent to CEFR level B2).
• Possess knowledge, skills, and competence relevant to one or more tasks described above.
• To possess adequate communication and representation skills.
• To possess at least two years of professional experience in one or more tasks described above.
Have experience in cooperating with third country diplomatic missions.
Specific to return and reintegration counselling (10.2.2.): •
Have experience in counselling activities regarding voluntary returns and reintegration.
• Have knowledge of procedures associated with voluntary return or reintegration.
Specific to use of return IT systems (10.2.3.): •
Have experience with return systems, databases and information management systems.
• Have knowledge of the technical aspects of EU MS return case management systems.
In addition, the following would be of advantage for all Return Specialists: •
Ability to verify the assertions of third-country nationals using specialised tools.
• Experience in cooperating with EU bodies, agencies and offices, Union funded programmes on return, international organisations and non-governmental organisations.
• Experience in providing strategic advice for the well-functioning of national return structures.
• Knowledge of other languages relevant to the tasks.
• Specific expertise in the protection of children and other persons in a vulnerable situation.
• Knowledge of inter-cultural communication and interviewing techniques.

A Crew Member is an official of a competent national authority of a MS 15 or a member of the Agency’s statutory staff responsible for the operation or maintenance of aerial or maritime assets who carries out at least one of the following tasks:

a) Management-level tasks associated with e.g. Master, Chief Officer (CO) or Chief Mate, Chief Engineer and First Engineer. The tasks of National Officials (for heavy technical equipment) as described in the respective operational plan should be executed by a crew member of this level.
b) Operational level tasks associated with e.g. officer in charge of a navigational watch, Engineer Officer and Radio Operator.
d) Boarding teams as member of the crew: border or coast guard officer part of the crew with assigned role and training in boarding: i)

To be able to perform boarding of the ships in case of unopposed and non-cooperative (up to passive resistance) boarding operations according to the classification of boarding operations within Frontex Joint Maritime Operations (Handbook on Boarding: Best Practices and Guidelines).
ii) If boarding team members are not part of the crew, the profile can be deployed on board of the ships, but it is advisable for the MS to deploy an entire boarding team. 11.2.2.

a) Management-level tasks associated with e.g. pilot in command, co-pilots, tactical coordinator or mission commander and maintenance officer or coordinator (depending on the respective competences). The tasks of National Officials (NO) mostly referred for heavy technical equipment, as described in the respective operational plan, should be executed by a crew member of this level or by any official that will be assigned by the MS national authority or the Agency correspondingly.16
b) Technical level tasks: Associated with e.g. sensor operators, flight engineers, rescue swimmers, mission support technicians.
c) Maintenance level tasks: Associated with e.g. first line and second line maintenance technician. 11.2.3.
a) To perform maintenance, renewal, and disposal of specialised technical equipment (patrol cars, vans, cameras, radars, etc).
b) To install, maintain and repair electronic, electrical, ICT, and mechanical equipment.
c) To carry out routine checks and tests and take corrective action where necessary.
d) To provide technical advice and support to stakeholders.
e) To troubleshoot and diagnose faults and malfunctions. f)
To monitor and control product configuration and carry out modifications and upgrades.
15 Crew Members provided by private contractors are excluded.
A Crew Member in the standing corps should: •
Possess knowledge, skills and competence relevant to the tasks described above.
• Possess a minimum of three years of experience in the specific crew role.
• Have adequate knowledge of the English language (equivalent to CEFR level B1 and at least B2 for management level).
• Be able to apply self-safety and security practices in accordance with defined standards and guidelines.
Be able to perform SAR activities in various distress situations at the sea borders in accordance with guidelines, tasks and relevant maritime law and best practices.
In addition, the following would be of advantage specifically for maritime assets (11.2.1.): •

Demonstrate experience and knowledge in performing coast guard functions within the scope of his or her role and tasks (e.g. fisheries inspections, environmental protection etc.) and possess good knowledge of relevant EU and international law.
• Be able to identify and report a series of cross-sectoral threats at the maritime domain.
12. Profiles to which the requirement to wear a uniform does not apply due to the specific nature of the operational activity

Unless formally instructed not to do so, the members of the European Border and Coast Guard standing corps shall wear a uniform when performing their tasks and exercising their powers. When, for reasons of service, the members of the standing corps perform tasks other than described under the profiles set out in this document or participate in institutional activities or events requiring a uniform, they shall wear a uniform unless they are deployed from a national authority which does not require its staff to wear a uniform.

Due to the specific nature of the operational activity, the obligation to wear the uniform does not apply when staff of the standing corps are performing specific tasks while deployed under the profiles listed in the subsections below. 12.2.1.

Staff of the standing corps deployed under the Border and Coast Guard Officer profile shall not wear a uniform when performing the following tasks as described under 2.3.3. (‘Return support (basic))’ unless requested by the host Member State and agreed in the respective operational plan. 12.2.2.

Staff of the standing corps deployed under the Debriefing Officer profile shall not wear a uniform when performing the tasks described under 4.2.1. (‘Debriefing and screening’) and 4.2.2. (‘Cultural mediation’). 12.2.3.
Frontex Return Escort and Support Officer

Staff of the standing corps deployed under the Frontex Return Escort and Support Officer profile shall not wear a uniform when performing any of the tasks described under 9.2., unless requested by the host Member State or the Agency and agreed in the respective operational plan. 12.2.4.

Staff of the standing corps deployed under the Return Specialist profile shall not wear a uniform when performing the tasks described under 10.2.1. (‘Third country cooperation’), 10.2.2. (‘Return and reintegration counselling’), and 10.2.3. (‘Use of return IT systems’).
